data.sourceWord: MCQ: Which of the following is karuna?

examples.en-GB: Answer: Compassion | Distractors: Wisdom; Impermanence; Mindfulness

data.targetWord: A Bodhisattva is an enlightened being who, out of great compassion (karuna), chooses to remain in the cycle of samsara rather than enter Nibbana, in order to help all other beings reach liberation.
A person becomes a Bodhisattva by perfecting six earthly attributes (generosity, morality, patience, energy, meditation, wisdom). Amitabha is the Bodhisattva of the Pure Land in Mahayana Buddhism.

Dependent arising (pratitya-samutpada) teaches that all phenomena arise in dependence on conditions; nothing exists independently. This influences Buddhists to recognise their interconnection with all living beings.
Since suffering arises from ignorance of dependent arising, understanding it enables Buddhists to loosen the chain of craving and aversion, making ethical, compassionate choices that reduce harm.
A Bodhisattva has generated bodhicitta ('Buddha mind') — the wish for all beings to be free from suffering. They combine compassion with wisdom, having the insight needed to guide others effectively.

data.sourceWord: Bodhisattva vow — remaining in samsara to help
data.targetWord: The Bodhisattva vow commits to remaining in the cycle of rebirth until all sentient beings are liberated. This act of selfless compassion is the highest expression of Mahayana Buddhist ethics.
'One road leads to wealth; another road leads to nirvana. Let the mendicant, the disciple of Buddha, learn this and not strive for honour but seek wisdom.' (Dhammapada 5:75)

data.sourceWord: FOR: Meditation is central to the Eightfold Path
data.targetWord: Three of the eight steps of the Noble Eightfold Path (Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, Right Concentration) relate directly to meditation. Without it, wisdom and morality cannot develop fully.

data.sourceWord: FOR: A still mind is the foundation of all Buddhist practice
data.targetWord: Samatha meditation develops the calm, focused mind that underpins all Buddhist practice. Nothing else in Buddhism is possible if the mind is restless; meditation is therefore the most important practice.

The Buddha taught the Eightfold Path in three clusters: morality (sila), meditation (samadhi), and wisdom (panna). Ethical behaviour is listed first because without a moral foundation, meditation cannot develop.

data.sourceWord: AGAINST: The Four Noble Truths are more fundamental
data.targetWord: The Four Noble Truths — the diagnosis of suffering and the prescription of the path — are the framework within which meditation operates. Understanding dukkha is more foundational than the practice of meditation.

data.answer: A Bodhisattva is an enlightened being who stays in samsara to help others.
Dependent arising teaches that all phenomena arise because of conditions.
Karuna means compassion for all living beings.

data.title: The Four Noble Truths
data.sourcePassage: The Four Noble Truths form the foundation of Buddhist teaching, first taught by the Buddha in his first sermon at the Deer Park in Sarnath. The First Noble Truth is dukkha — the truth of suffering. Life involves unsatisfactory experiences, from physical pain to the frustration of not getting what we want. The Second Noble Truth is samudaya — the origin of suffering. Suffering arises from craving (tanha): craving for pleasure, for existence, and for non-existence. The Third Noble Truth is nirodha — the cessation of suffering. It is possible to end suffering by eliminating craving; this state of liberation is called Nibbana. The Fourth Noble Truth is magga — the path to the cessation of suffering, namely the Noble Eightfold Path. This practical path of right understanding, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration leads to liberation. The Four Noble Truths are not merely beliefs but a diagnosis and treatment plan that Buddhists are encouraged to test in their own experience.
